difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (drug → reduced inflammation → improved outcomes). The correct weakener attacks the move from evidence to conclusion by introducing an alternative explanation for the observed improvement. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope trap about a different drug.
stimulus: A clinical researcher concluded that a new anti-inflammatory drug was responsible for the significant reduction in joint pain reported by patients in a recent trial. Patients who took the drug for eight weeks reported a 40 percent decrease in pain scores compared to their scores at the start of the trial. No other treatments were administered during the study period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The trial did not include a control group of patients who received a placebo instead of the drug.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug's active compound has been shown in laboratory studies to inhibit the specific enzyme responsible for inflammation in joint tissue.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A different anti-inflammatory drug tested in a separate trial produced only a 25 percent decrease in pain scores over the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several participants in the trial began a low-impact exercise program during the eight-week period without informing the research team.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients with more severe joint pain at the start of the trial reported greater absolute reductions in pain scores than those with milder initial pain.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes the drug caused the pain reduction. Choice D introduces an alternative explanation—an independent exercise program—that could account for the improved pain scores, directly undermining the causal attribution to the drug.
explanations.A: This is a strengthener trap: the absence of a control group actually weakens the researcher's methodology and might seem to weaken the argument, but on LSAT logic the question is whether A, if true, undermines the conclusion. Absence of a placebo group weakens the evidentiary basis—however, D is a more direct weakener because it supplies an actual competing cause rather than merely noting a methodological gap. Among the choices, D most directly attacks the causal conclusion by introducing a specific confounding variable.
explanations.B: Opposite/strengthener trap. Demonstrating a mechanism by which the drug suppresses inflammation bolsters the causal claim rather than undermining it.
explanations.C: Unwarranted-comparison trap. The argument concerns whether this drug caused the improvement; the relative performance of a different drug is irrelevant to that causal claim.
explanations.D: Correct. Introduces a concrete alternative cause (exercise) that could explain the pain reduction independent of the drug.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant trap. The distribution of improvement across severity levels does not challenge the claim that the drug caused improvement overall; it merely describes a pattern within the results.

difficultyReason: Predictive argument: an economist predicts future economic growth based on a historical correlation. The weakener attacks the move from past correlation to future prediction by undermining the stability of the underlying condition. One distractor strengthens; another attacks a premise without touching the conclusion.
stimulus: An economist argued that the city of Harwell will experience significant economic growth over the next decade. Harwell recently completed a large-scale expansion of its public transit network, and historical data from twelve other cities show that comparable transit expansions were each followed within five years by measurable increases in commercial investment and employment rates.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the economist's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The twelve cities cited by the economist all completed their transit expansions during periods of broad national economic growth, whereas Harwell's expansion was completed during a national recession.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Harwell's transit expansion was completed under budget and on schedule, suggesting strong project management capacity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two of the twelve cities experienced their economic growth only eight years after the transit expansion, rather than within five years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some economists dispute whether increases in commercial investment are the best measure of economic growth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Harwell's transit expansion added more total route-miles than any of the twelve comparable expansions cited by the economist.

explanations.correct: The economist's prediction depends on the historical pattern holding for Harwell. Choice A reveals that all twelve comparison cities expanded during national economic upturns, while Harwell did so during a recession—exposing a critical disanalogy that undermines the reliability of the historical pattern as a predictor for Harwell's future.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the analogical reasoning at the heart of the prediction by showing the comparison cases were conducted under systematically different macroeconomic conditions.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Demonstrating Harwell's organizational competence makes a successful outcome more likely, bolstering rather than weakening the economist's prediction.
explanations.C: Too-narrow trap. The two-year delay in a minority of cases is a minor variation that does not undermine the general pattern; the economist's claim is about the next decade, so a slight timing difference is irrelevant to whether growth will occur.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. Debating the best metric for economic growth challenges a definitional premise but does not undermine whether Harwell will experience growth as the economist defines it.
explanations.E: Unwarranted-comparison trap that actually functions as a mild strengthener—Harwell's larger expansion might predict even greater growth—so it does not weaken the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Causal-generalization argument in environmental science. The argument moves from a single regional observation to a broad policy conclusion. The correct weakener challenges the representativeness of the evidence by showing the observed outcome results from a local factor that does not generalize. Distractors include one strengthener and one irrelevant trap.
stimulus: A conservation official argued that reintroducing gray wolves to wilderness areas is an effective strategy for restoring native plant diversity. In Ridgecrest Valley, where wolves were reintroduced seven years ago, the populations of elk and deer declined sharply, grazing pressure on riverbank vegetation was reduced, and the density of native shrubs and grasses increased by over 60 percent.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ridgecrest Valley contains an unusually high concentration of natural mineral springs that independently promote rapid plant growth in riparian zones.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gray wolves in Ridgecrest Valley have expanded their territory to areas outside the original reintroduction zone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several wilderness areas lacking large predators have experienced significant declines in native plant diversity over the same seven-year period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reintroduction of gray wolves required a ten-year planning process and cooperation among multiple government agencies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The elk population in Ridgecrest Valley had already begun declining slightly before the wolves were reintroduced, due to a drought the previous year.

explanations.correct: The official generalizes from Ridgecrest Valley's outcome to a broad strategy. Choice A reveals that Ridgecrest Valley has an idiosyncratic feature—mineral springs that accelerate plant growth—that could independently account for the observed increase in plant diversity. This alternative explanation undercuts the conclusion that wolf reintroduction itself was the effective driver, and suggests the result may not generalize to other wilderness areas.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a site-specific confounding variable (mineral springs) that could explain the plant diversity increase independent of the wolves, both providing an alternative explanation and undermining the generalizability of the single case.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant trap. The wolves' territorial expansion does not address whether their presence caused the plant diversity increase or whether the strategy works elsewhere.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Showing that areas without predators fared worse over the same period supports the comparative case for wolf reintroduction, bolstering the official's argument.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. The difficulty and cost of the planning process bears on the policy's feasibility, not on whether wolf reintroduction effectively restores plant diversity.
explanations.E: Too-narrow / premise-attack trap. A pre-existing slight elk decline would weaken the wolf-caused-elk-decline link, but since some decline did still occur and plant diversity did increase, this choice does not substantially undercut the conclusion that the strategy produced the plant diversity outcome.
